nameStory: New England boneset gets its name from both its limited range and the old belief that boneset plants could heal broken bones. Early settlers and Native Americans used various boneset species to treat fevers and aches, thinking they could literally help bones 'set' properly, though we now know they don't actually mend fractures.
description: New England boneset is a tall, upright wildflower that can tower over 3 feet high in late summer. It produces distinctive flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers that look like miniature daisies but lack the familiar white petals. This rare plant is found only in a few counties of southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, making it one of New England's most geographically restricted wildflowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white flower heads, each containing only 5-7 small disc florets with no ray petals - imagine a daisy center without the white petals around it

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a smooth texture and pointed tips that feel papery when dried

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy perennial that stands erect and can reach over 3 feet in height, with multiple branching stems topped by the flower clusters

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Upright stems that feel firm and somewhat woody at the base, branching near the top to support the flat flower clusters

habitat: New England boneset grows in very specific locations within just four counties in southeastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island. It thrives in sandy coastal plain habitats, often in areas with well-drained soils and full to partial sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground as the weather warms, developing into leafy stems throughout late spring.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive flat-topped white flower clusters bloom in late summer, typically August through early September, attracting various small pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce small, fluffy seeds that disperse on the wind, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back to the ground completely, leaving no above-ground parts visible until spring regrowth.

funFact: This plant is actually a hybrid that formed naturally between two other boneset species, then became so successful at reproducing on its own that scientists now consider it a completely separate species - it's essentially evolution creating a new plant in our backyard!
confusionNotes: New England boneset was mistakenly identified as the more common white-bracted boneset for many years until DNA testing revealed it was actually a completely different species. The key difference is the geographic range - if you're seeing it outside of southeastern Massachusetts or Rhode Island, it's definitely not New England boneset.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents a fascinating case of botanical detective work, where plants collected for decades were reclassified as a new species in 2005 after DNA analysis revealed they weren't related to what botanists originally thought. It's also listed as endangered in both Massachusetts and Rhode Island due to its extremely limited range.
compareHints: Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves. It also differs from other bonesets by its very restricted coastal range in just four counties, whereas most other boneset species are found across much wider areas of New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base.

Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.

Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves.
Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves.
Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
